If you want to “sway” your investing results ethically, focus on factors you can control: your research process, your risk management, and your time horizon. Instead of trying to move prices, you can seek opportunities where you believe the market is mispricing a company based on public information, then invest accordingly. Over time, prices may change as more information becomes widely understood—this is different from trying to force a price move.

A reproducible approach is to define clear criteria for selecting investments (e.g., profitability, debt levels, valuation), test those criteria on historical data, and apply strict position sizing so that no single trade can significantly harm your portfolio. You can also diversify, use limit orders to control execution price, and avoid illiquid assets where spreads and slippage can dominate returns.

Finally, keep records. A trading journal that logs your thesis, entry/exit points, and results helps you improve decision-making. This “sways” outcomes in your favor by improving discipline and reducing avoidable errors—without attempting to manipulate the market.

### Example (reproducible code: a simple, lawful screening workflow)

import yfinance as yf
import pandas as pd

tickers = ["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "AMZN", "TSLA"]
data = yf.download(tickers, period="2y")["Adj Close"]

# Compute simple momentum: 6-month return
six_month_days = 126  # approx trading days
returns_6m = data.pct_change(six_month_days).iloc[-1].sort_values(ascending=False)

# Pick top 2 by 6-month momentum (purely based on public price data)
selected = returns_6m.head(2)

print("6-month returns:")
print(returns_6m)

print("\nSelected tickers:")
print(selected.index.tolist())

# Basic risk control idea: equal-weight the selected names
weights = pd.Series(1/len(selected), index=selected.index)
print("\nPortfolio weights:")
print(weights)
